name: Opus-fleet dividend growth
strategy: Concentrated in 25+ year dividend aristocrats and quality dividend-grower ETFs with defensive staples/healthcare tilt, funded by strong free cash flow, harvesting 4% cash yield on the sleeve.

positions.thesis: Core anchor, raised from 33% to 36%. Head-to-head against its two rivals this week SCHD wins on every axis that matters to this mandate: +31.73% trailing 1yr total return versus DGRO's +25.21% and NOBL's +16.32%, a 3.09% yield versus 1.86% and 1.99%, and a 0.06% fee versus 0.08% and 0.35%. It now holds $105.7B across 103 quality-screened dividend growers. I am removing three single names this week, and routing part of that weight into the diversified basket rather than into another single name lowers idiosyncratic and earnings-date risk while keeping the quality-income factor exposure fully intact. Deep 12% stop is portfolio-level protection only, not a trading stop on a 103-name basket.

Upsized from 8% to 11% and now my largest single name. Last week I explicitly refused to add because the Jul 31 print was a genuine coin flip; it landed on the right side — adj EPS $3.65 versus $3.61 consensus, management calling it 'another excellent quarter,' FY26 revenue guidance RAISED to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, Skyrizi momentum in immunology, EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata and FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing. Yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 Buy consensus, +11.1%. A 53-year raise streak at a 2.81% yield where the event risk is banked and the price is lower than before the event is the single best risk-adjusted setup in my universe. The stop widens from 10% to 12% precisely because the earnings binary that justified the tight stop no longer exists.

Upsized from 8% to 9% and now the larger of my two energy legs. A 38-year raiser yielding 3.82% — the highest yield in the entire book — at 12.21x forward earnings, with quarterly net income of $12.1B against $2.5B a year ago and a $216.96 consensus implying 16.3% upside. Against XOM's identical oil-price driver it pays 113 basis points more income for six more points of upside at a cheaper multiple, so if I want energy I want it here. Held to single digits rather than pushed harder because the earnings are levered to a Middle East geopolitical premium that can deflate overnight, it fell 1.41% on a day the S&P rose 0.61%, and there is active political pressure on the company to cut pump prices. The 10% stop stays because this is the one leg whose thesis has a genuine one-headline reversal risk.

Trimmed from 13% to 9%. The company is doing nothing wrong — 5% volume and 6% organic revenue growth, FY guidance raised, EPS +18% year over year, FIFA World Cup engagement, and a 62-year King's streak intact. What changed is the price: at $87.05 against a $94.70 consensus the upside has compressed from roughly 17% at entry to about 9%, it trades at 26.2x for a 2.44% yield, and it sits close to its $90.92 52-week high while the staples complex it belongs to has returned only 7.18% over a year. This remains the best staple I own and I keep a real weight in it, but it no longer earns a 13% slot when the reward per unit of risk has more than halved. The take-profit drops from +20% to +12% because a +20% target was never going to fill from here.

New position, funded by the P&G exit. A 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat yielding 3.30% — the richest yield available among healthcare aristocrats — with a 0.57 beta, FY26 revenue up 8.43% to $36.36B, and a Buy consensus at $98.44 against $87.16, or 12.9% upside. It trades in the bottom third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, so I am buying defensive quality on sale rather than chasing. Pipeline is moving: expanded CE Mark for the Affera mapping and ablation system into ventricular arrhythmias, plus closed acquisitions of SPR Therapeutics and Scientia Vascular. Decisively, it does not report until Sep 1, so unlike every other name I own this quarter it carries no near-term earnings binary — it is pure ballast. This is how I replace P&G's defensive role while moving it into the sector that is actually compounding, XLV +29.17% against XLP +7.18%.

Trimmed from 9% to 7%. The fundamental case is unchanged and good — a 53-year raiser that beat with adj EPS $1.31 and raised FY EPS guidance, with FDA clearance to commercialize the SimpleScreen blood-based colorectal test opening a new diagnostics market, and the DOJ criminal probe into the formula facility now closed, which removes a legal overhang. I trim rather than hold flat for two specific reasons: at 34.9x trailing the consensus offers only 9.84% upside to $118.42, and Abbott is currently investigating cyber incidents affecting its cancer diagnostics business and internal systems, which is a live operational unknown with no quantified cost. I also already own it indirectly at 4.64% of SCHD, my largest position, so 7% direct is closer to 9% effective exposure. The take-profit comes in from +18% to +15% to sit nearer where the sell-side actually is.

Trimmed from 7% to 6% and deliberately kept behind CVX. The quarter was excellent in absolute terms — $14.5B of earnings on $23.6B of operating cash flow driven by Guyana and Permian volumes, with TD Cowen raising its target to $168 from $155 — and it remains a 40+ year raiser with enormous free cash flow. But it yields 2.69% against Chevron's 3.82% and offers roughly 10% upside against Chevron's 16.3% off the identical crude-price driver, so within a fixed energy budget every dollar is better spent next door. I keep a real position rather than exiting because I want diversified energy exposure across two operators, not a single-company bet on one asset base. Total energy sits at 15%, unchanged in size but improved in mix.

Held flat at 5%. I trimmed this to half size last week on the FY26 EPS guidance cut and the talc exposure, and that fear has not compounded: the $5.5B talc settlement is now a settled and quantified number rather than an open liability across roughly 76,000 suits, the stock closed up 0.88% at $259.24, OTTAVA robotic surgery has launched, Rybrevant Faspro received FDA priority review, and multiple analysts have raised targets. I do not add back, because at a $272.50 consensus there is only 5.12% upside left and Goldman has pulled it from its conviction list while keeping the Buy. This is a 63-year Dividend King held as low-beta ballast, sized for what it is. No take-profit attached — with the consensus this close, a TP would simply fire on noise and cost me the ballast I am holding it for. Wide 12% stop for the same reason.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three names have had their theses actually falsified by news this week and one had its thesis confirmed while the price fell, so I am reallocating along the evidence rather than sitting still. PG goes to zero: a 68-year raise streak does not offset a Q4 miss, missed organic sales, two fresh downgrades to Hold, guided Q1 EPS down 5%+, and a $3.8B Thorne acquisition that spends shareholder cash outside the core while the core decelerates — and XLP at +7.18% over a year against XLV at +29.17% says the entire complex is dead money. ADP goes to zero on the cleanest signal I found all week: ADP's own employment report shows July job creation of 44,000, the weakest in six months, and ADP bills per employee on client payrolls, so its own data is a leading indicator against its own revenue, with consensus already at Hold and only 5.66% upside. MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works. Against those cuts I add ABBV, which beat at $3.65 vs $3.61 and RAISED FY26 revenue guidance yet trades 11% below target, because a resolved-favourably earnings event that leaves the stock cheaper is the exact setup I underweighted for last week. I open MDT, a 48-year aristocrat at a 3.30% yield and 0.57 beta in the bottom third of its range with no print until Sep 1, which buys back the defensive ballast PG was supposed to provide but does it in the sector that is actually working. I tilt energy toward CVX over XOM because CVX pays 113bps more yield at 12.2x forward with 16.3% upside versus 10% for the same oil-price driver. Finally I lift the SCHD anchor to 36% and carry 10% cash: with three single names removed, pushing weight into the one instrument that out-yields, out-returns and out-costs both DGRO and NOBL cuts idiosyncratic risk without giving up the factor, and holding dry powder at 4% risk-free while the index closes within 0.5% of its all-time high amid record options activity is the mandate's own cash sleeve doing its job.
novelty: I manage no Round-2 book in this experiment, so the <50% same-direction overlap constraint has no counterparty to bind against; what distinguishes this book on its own terms is that it is the only long-only, zero-leverage, zero-crypto sleeve here whose entire edge is 25+ year dividend-raise streaks bought at consensus discounts, and this week it deliberately rotates staples weight into healthcare aristocrats — cutting P&G and McDonald's outright to fund AbbVie and Medtronic — rather than joining the gold-miner and leveraged-semi squeeze trades that dominated the tape.
research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED (200/200) BEFORE I STARTED, so all research was done via WebFetch on stockanalysis.com quote/fund pages, which carry 2026-08-07 closing marks, TTM fundamentals, consensus targets and recent-news digests. Coverage was complete: I pulled every one of my ten holdings plus three replacement candidates and three market/sector benchmarks.

MARKET BACKDROP (8/7 close): SPY $773.26, +0.61% on the day, 52wk high $776.85 — the index closed within 0.5% of its all-time high, YTD +23.55%, with news flow citing record options activity and "S&P to 8,000 before year-end" chatter. That is a melt-up tape, not a defensive one, which explains why my book returned only +1.15% on the week. Sector split is the important finding: XLV (healthcare) +29.17% 1yr, beta 0.56, described in coverage as "a haven for investors" on earnings momentum and rotation out of tech; XLP (staples) only +7.18% 1yr. Both halves of my "defensive staples/healthcare" mandate are permitted, but one is compounding at 4x the other. That asymmetry drives most of what follows.

CORE INSTRUMENT CHECK: SCHD $33.90, +31.73% 1yr total return, 3.09% yield, 0.06% fee, $105.7B AUM (up from $100B), 103 holdings, top names ABT 4.64%/AMGN 4.61%/HD 4.31%. I benchmarked it against the two alternatives: DGRO +25.21% 1yr at a 1.86% yield, NOBL +16.32% 1yr at a 1.99% yield and a 0.35% fee. SCHD beats both on return AND yield AND cost, so the anchor stays SCHD and gets bigger rather than diversified across wrappers.

WHAT RESOLVED WELL: ABBV reported adj EPS $3.65 vs $3.61 consensus, called it "another excellent quarter," RAISED FY26 revenue guidance to ~$67.6B from $67.3B, flagged Skyrizi momentum, and added EC approval for Rinvoq in alopecia areata plus FDA acceptance of a supplemental Botox Cosmetic filing — yet the stock sits at $246.04 against a $273.39 target (+11.1%) and a 2.81% yield. The coin-flip print I refused to upsize into last week landed on the right side and the price went the wrong way. JNJ $259.24 (+0.88% on the day): the talc overhang is now a settled $5.5B number, OTTAVA launched, Rybrevant Faspro got FDA priority review, multiple targets were raised — the guidance-cut fear I trimmed on did not compound.

WHAT DETERIORATED: (1) PG $145.79, sitting near its 52wk low of $137.62 against a $167.25 high. Q4 missed, organic sales missed, HSBC AND Argus both cut to Hold, management blamed "rising input costs" and "economic and geopolitical uncertainty," and Q1 EPS is guided to decline 5%+. On top of a decelerating core they are spending $3.8B on Thorne, a supplements maker — capital leaving the core franchise while the core is shrinking. (2) ADP $271.32, consensus now HOLD with only 5.66% upside. The decisive item is that ADP's own National Employment Report shows US businesses added just 44,000 jobs in July, the smallest in six months. ADP bills on pays-per-control, so its own published data is a leading indicator against its own revenue line. (3) MCD reported 8/4: value-menu rollout execution failure, weak deal promotion, a pullback in digital offers, an outright drop in visits, and a new US president (Skye Anderson) installed to fix it. Multiple targets cut. (4) ABT $107.81 at 34.9x trailing with only 9.84% upside, and coverage flags Abbott investigating cyber incidents affecting cancer diagnostics and internal systems — a live operational unknown.

ENERGY: CVX $186.56, 3.82% yield, 12.21x forward, net income $12.1B vs $2.5B a year ago, consensus $216.96 (+16.3%). XOM $153.04, 2.69% yield, Q2 earnings $14.5B on $23.6B operating cash flow from Guyana/Permian, TD Cowen to $168, but only ~10% upside. Same sector, same driver — CVX pays 113bps more yield for 6pts more upside at a cheaper multiple. Both rest on a Middle East geopolitical premium and CVX fell 1.41% on a day the tape rose 0.61%, plus coverage notes political pressure on pump prices, so this is the leg I keep stopped rather than upsized aggressively.

REPLACEMENT SOURCED: MDT $87.16, a 48-consecutive-year Dividend Aristocrat, 3.30% yield — the highest-yielding healthcare aristocrat I could find — trading in the lower third of a $73.31-$106.33 range, consensus Buy at $98.44 (+12.9%), beta 0.57, FY26 revenue +8.43%, with Affera mapping/ablation CE Mark expanded to ventricular arrhythmias and SPR Therapeutics plus Scientia Vascular closed. Critically, it does not report until Sep 1, so it carries no near-term earnings binary.

NOT APPLICABLE TO ME: the tape warning on GDX/GDXJ/SOXL short squeezes is irrelevant here — this book is long-only equity with zero gold, zero leveraged ETFs, zero crypto and zero perps.
